text:
On April 27, 2018, DocuSign listed on NASDAQ. The IPO had been priced at $29 a share. Three and a half years later, in September 2021, the stock touched $310. The pandemic had remade DocuSign from a steady B2B e-signature company into one of the most valuable software stocks of the COVID era. Then the demand curve normalized. Eighteen months later, DocuSign traded at $39. The company had cycled through two CEOs, three rounds of layoffs, an activist investor, and a collapsed take-private bid. This video is about the math underneath that arc. It is not a video about e-signature. It is a video about the gap between subscription growth and subscription health.

DocuSign filed its first 10-K as a public company in March 2019. Annual revenue was $701 million, up 35% year over year. That was the steady SaaS profile. Two fiscal years later, the company reported $1.453 billion in revenue, up 49%. By fiscal 2022, the year that ended January 2022, revenue had reached $2.107 billion, up another 45%. Headcount tracked the curve. From approximately 2,400 employees at the IPO, DocuSign grew past 7,300 by early 2023. Most of that hiring landed in sales, customer success, and engineering. Each new salesperson was assumed to ramp within four to six quarters. Each engineer was building against a product roadmap drawn at peak demand. Then-CEO Dan Springer told investors on multiple earnings calls that the demand environment had structurally shifted.

DocuSign's customer base nearly doubled between fiscal 2020 and fiscal 2021. On the Q4 fiscal 2021 earnings call in March 2021, the company reported its largest sequential expansion of customer count in its history as a public company. Enterprise customers, the higher-margin tier, grew sharply year over year. Contract durations stretched. Average contract value rose. Every leading indicator on the dashboard was pointing up. The Agreement Cloud rebrand, announced in 2019, had positioned the company to capture an addressable market beyond e-signature. The pandemic delivered the demand without requiring the strategic execution.

The early signal was billings, not revenue. Billings are the leading indicator in a subscription business. They reflect contracts signed in the current period, not revenue ratably recognized from prior periods. By the second quarter of fiscal 2023, reported in September 2022, DocuSign billings growth had dropped into the single digits while revenue growth was still in the low twenties. The gap was the lag. Customers who had signed expensive long-term contracts in 2020 were renewing at lower seat counts or not renewing at all. The unit economics modeled at peak demand were drawn from cohorts that had been forced into the product by remote-work mandate, not by deliberate choice.

Inside DocuSign, the change was felt in the quarterly planning cycle. Revenue targets that had been raised through 2021 began holding flat. Hiring requisitions slowed and then froze. The product roadmap shifted from growth features to retention features. Sales compensation plans were rewritten to weight renewal performance over new logo acquisition. By the time the public financial statements caught up, the strategic posture had already changed inside the building.

In June 2022, Dan Springer stepped down. The official language was a mutual decision with the board. The substantive change came four months later. In October 2022, DocuSign announced Allan Thygesen as the new chief executive. Thygesen had spent fifteen years at Google, most recently running the Americas advertising business. DocuSign was reportedly his first public-company CEO role. The hiring of an ads operator to run a sales-led B2B SaaS company was itself a signal. The board was no longer optimizing for hyper-growth. It was optimizing for go-to-market efficiency.
